search.x: On a scoring play, a double adds 5 points. When your scoring play uses a double (both halves show the same number, including the double blank), the play gains +5 points for each copy . Only the bone you just played is checked, not the doubles already on the table. The open ends must still add up to a multiple of five; Double Trouble only adds to a play that already scores. Pairs naturally with Golden Double , which then doubles the whole play including this bonus, and with Collector . Cracked Doubles takes 5 points per copy back from any scoring double. On a scoring play, a bone containing a blank adds 5 points. When your scoring play uses a bone with at least one blank half (0-1 through 0-6, and the double blank), the play gains +5 points for each copy . A blank that played as a wild card still counts as a blank bone. Combines well with Wild Blank and Counterfeit Pip , which make blanks much easier to place.

A scoring play made immediately after drawing adds 5 points. Your first play after a trip to the boneyard gains +5 points for each copy if it scores. It works whether you play the bone you just drew or another one. If the drawn bone cannot play, your turn passes, and the bonus waits for your next play. Using a Table Pass also counts as a trip for this perk. Any play clears the bonus, scoring or not, so only that one play can earn it.

On a scoring play, a bone with 3 total pips or fewer adds 5 points. When your scoring play uses a bone with 3 pips or fewer in total (0-0, 0-1, 0-2, 0-3, 1-1 and 1-2), the play gains +5 points for each copy .

On a scoring play, a bone with an odd pip total adds 5 points. When your scoring play uses a bone whose two halves add up to an odd number (for example 2-3 or 1-6), the play gains +5 points for each copy . Holding both Odd Job and Even Flow guarantees one of them fires on every scoring play.

On a scoring play, a bone with an even pip total adds 5 points. When your scoring play uses a bone whose two halves add up to an even number (every double, plus bones such as 1-3 or 2-6), the play gains +5 points for each copy . The double blank (0 pips) counts as even.

Your first scoring play of each round adds 5 points. Your first play of each hand that actually scores gains +5 points for each copy . "Actually scores" means points were added to your score. A play that a malus reduced to zero (such as Five Jinx on a total of 5) does not use up First Blood; it waits for your next scoring play. It resets at the start of every hand.

Your remaining hand awards your opponent 5 fewer points. When you lose a hand , the points your remaining bones give the winner are reduced by 5 for each copy , before the award is rounded to a multiple of five. The award can never drop below zero. It works on blocked hands as well as when the winner goes domino. It applies after Bone Fortress 's cap and before maluses such as Heavy Hand and Exposed Hand . See the hand award order on Scoring in depth . Worked example You lose holding 6-5 and 3-2: 16 pips. With one Soft Landing the award is 16 - 5 = 11, which rounds up to 15 instead of 20.

A scoring play with an open-end total of exactly 5 adds another 5 points. A scoring play whose open ends add up to exactly 5 gains +5 points for each copy , so a single copy turns a 5-point play into 10. Five Jinx wipes out a play that totals exactly 5, bonus included. The Long Charge also pays out on a total of exactly 5, so the two work together.

After losing a hand, your first scoring play next hand adds 5 points per stack. After you lose a hand , your first scoring play of the next hand gains +5 points for each copy you held when the hand was lost. The bonus is spent by your first play of the new hand whose open ends add up to a multiple of five, even if a malus reduces that play. Winning a hand clears it. Losing two hands in a row does not build up two bonuses.

A scoring play that is your second or later consecutive play without visiting the boneyard adds 5 points. A scoring play gains +5 points for each copy when it is your second or later play in a row without visiting the boneyard . The streak counts your own plays only; Rival's turns in between do not break it. Drawing from the boneyard, using a Table Pass , or passing because the boneyard is empty resets the streak. So does the start of a new hand. Your very first play after a reset never qualifies.
A scoring play made while you are behind adds 5 points. A scoring play gains +5 points for each copy when your match score is lower than Rival's at the moment you play. Being tied does not count.

Every time you go to the boneyard, one fixed face-down bone is revealed. Every time you go to the boneyard, one face-down bone in the boneyard is turned face-up for you before you choose. You still pick which bone to take, so you can take the revealed one or avoid it. The revealed bone is the next bone in the boneyard's fixed order, so it is shown again on later visits until someone takes it. Extra copies do not reveal more bones. This is a passive perk. It is a different thing from the Boneyard Lantern supply, which lights up one random bone for a single trip.

Once per round, draw two bones and keep the one with fewer pips. On a boneyard visit, you turn over one extra face-down bone : you pick two, both are revealed, and you keep the one with fewer pips . The other stays in the boneyard. If both have the same pip total, you choose. It is used automatically on your first boneyard visit of each hand. Each copy gives one such visit per hand. On a visit that Sovereign Draw , Dead Man's Draw or Greedy Draw already changes, Light Fingers sits out and keeps its use for a later visit. It needs at least one spare bone in the boneyard beyond what you must tak

Whenever a malus lowers a scoring play, restore up to 5 points per stack. When a malus lowers one of your scoring plays, Pip Shield gives back up to 5 of the lost points for each copy . It covers Cracked Doubles , Five Jinx and Perk Tax , the maluses that act on a scoring play. It never gives back more than the maluses took from that play. It does nothing for maluses that act elsewhere, such as Leaky Pocket or the hand award maluses. Worked example You play a total of 5 with Five Alive (5 + 5 = 10) while holding Five Jinx . Five Jinx takes all 10 points. One Pip Shield restores 5, so the play

A scoring play on a vertical branch adds 5 points. A scoring play gains +5 points for each copy when you play on a vertical branch : the arms that grow up and down from a spinner after its long sides are filled. Every bone further along an upward or downward arm counts too. Plays on the main left and right line do not qualify.

Once per round, choose one of your bones and one face-down boneyard bone to swap. On your turn, choose one of your bones and one face-down boneyard bone, and they trade places. You don't see the new bone until it lands in your hand. Each copy gives one swap per hand. Using it does not end your turn: you can still play or draw afterwards. The bone you give away goes back into the boneyard face-down. It needs at least one bone in the boneyard.

Once per round, replace a drawn bone worth at least 10 pips. When you draw from the boneyard and pick a heavy bone (10 or more pips) , Salvager lets you pick one more face-down bone, turns them over, and you keep the one you want . Each copy covers one heavy draw per hand. It only triggers when the boneyard still has another bone to offer. The heavy bones are 4-6, 5-5, 5-6 and 6-6.

Once per hand, reveal one hidden bone of your choice to reveal a random hidden opponent bone. Both racks need at least three bones; revealed bones stay public while held. Once per hand, choose one of your own hidden bones to reveal to Rival. In return, one of Rival's hidden bones is chosen at random and revealed to you. Both racks need at least three bones, and each needs at least one bone that is still hidden. Revealed bones stay face-up for as long as their owner holds them, so Rival can see the bone you showed. More copies do not give more uses; it stays once per hand.

Once per hand, after an ordinary unplayable draw, return that bone face-up to its original boneyard position and end your turn. No replacement draw. When an ordinary boneyard draw gives you a bone that cannot be played , you may put it back face-up in the exact spot it came from and end your turn instead of keeping it. You get no replacement draw; your turn simply ends with your hand unchanged. The draw still counts as a draw: streaks reset and Leaky Pocket still charges you. The returned bone stays face-up in the boneyard, so both players can see it and whoever draws that spot gets it. "Ordin

Once per hand per stack, drag one pip across a bone's divider. Values stay within 0–6. The shifted bone becomes public and must be played this turn. Once per hand for each copy, drag one pip across a bone's divider : one half loses a pip and the other gains it. The total stays the same, and no half can go below 0 or above 6. Doubles can be split too (3-3 can become 2-4). The game only lets you confirm a change that makes the bone playable right now. The shifted bone becomes public (Rival sees it), and you must play it this turn . You cannot draw or play another bone first. Perks then see the s

Once per round, choose one of your bones and one face-down opponent bone to swap blindly. On your turn, choose one of your bones and one of Rival's face-down bones, and they trade places. You pick Rival's bone blind. After the trade both bones are public : you can see what you received and Rival can see what you gave away. Each copy gives one swap per hand. Using it does not end your turn. Turncoat is the legendary version that shows you Rival's whole rack first.

Once per round, arm a one-pip-away placement, preview its +1 or -1 change, and spend the charge only when played. Arm Loaded End on your turn, then you may play a bone on an end it misses by exactly one pip (for example a 4 against an open 5 or 3). The placement preview keeps a +1 or −1 cue visible before you commit. The status column shows the armed perk and remaining uses once. The charge is only spent when you actually make a play that would otherwise be illegal. If you make an ordinary play instead, the arming is cancelled and the charge is kept. Click the perk again to disarm it for free.

Once per round, arm one blank as a wildcard, preview its wild placement, and spend the charge only when played. Arm Counterfeit Pip, then one of your blank bones may be played on any open end as if its blank matched. A compact icon marks affected landing previews. The status column shows the armed perk and remaining uses; hover or focus a landing for the outcome. The double blank takes the end's value on both halves, so 0-0 played on a 4 becomes a 4-4 for the open ends and for scoring. The charge is only spent by a play that would not have been legal anyway. Once per draft per stack, upgrade the lower-rarity perk offer by one rarity tier. Once per draft for each copy, upgrade the lowest-rarity positive card in the offer by one rarity tier: Common to Uncommon, Uncommon to Rare, and so on. The new card is a random perk of that tier that you have unlocked. Online, it can be any perk of that tier the match allows, so an Epic card can become a Legendary one. It never upgrades the Malus card, and it never creates a second copy of a card already offered at the new tier. A Legendary card cannot be upgraded further. It is not available in All In or Legenda
A scoring play with an open-end total of at least 25 adds 20 points. A scoring play whose open ends add up to 25 or more gains +20 points for each copy .

On a scoring play, each distinct double you have played this round adds 2 points. On a scoring play, gain +2 points for every different double you have played this hand , for each copy. The double you are playing right now counts if it is new. Playing the same double value twice only counts once; the count resets every hand. Worked example You have already played 1-1 and 5-5 this hand and now score with 3-3. That is three different doubles: +6 with one Collector, +12 with two.
A scoring play with the 6-6 bone adds 30 points. A scoring play made with the 6-6 gains +30 points for each copy .

Each consecutive scoring play adds 5 more points than the previous scoring play. Each scoring play gains +5 points for every scoring play you made in a row just before it , for each copy. Your first scoring play of a streak gains nothing, the second gains +5, the third +10, and so on. The streak breaks when you make a play that doesn't score, when you draw from the boneyard, and at the start of every hand. Rival's plays don't break it. Worked example Three scoring plays in a row with one Domino Effect: +0, then +5, then +10. With two copies: +0, +10, +20.

Your remaining hand can award your opponent no more than 10 points. When you lose a hand, your remaining bones can award the winner at most 10 points . The cap is applied first; Soft Landing then reduces it further, and Heavy Hand and Exposed Hand can push it back up. Extra copies change nothing.

Going domino doubles the opposing hand award. When you go domino (play your last bone), the award you collect from Rival's remaining bones is doubled for each copy : two copies make it four times as large. It only works when you go domino, not when you win a blocked hand. The doubled award is rounded up to a multiple of five.

A scoring play with a double doubles the entire play. A scoring play made with a double is doubled in full for each copy: the open-end total, every perk bonus and the Midas Touch extra all double. Two copies make the play four times as large. It happens after the perk bonuses are added and before The Equalizer and any maluses. See Scoring in depth . Worked example You play 5-5 and the ends total 20, with Double Trouble : 20 + 5 = 25. Golden Double makes it 50 .

Your blanks may match any open end. Your blank bones may be played on any open end . A blank half matches whatever number it touches; the other half stays as printed. The double blank takes the end's value on both halves (0-0 played on a 3 plays as a 3-3). It is permanent and needs no arming. Extra copies change nothing. Counterfeit Pip is the one-use version.

Once per round, choose a bone and change each value to its double-six complement. Choose one of your bones and change each half to its double-six complement : every number becomes 6 minus itself. A 1-4 becomes 5-2, a 6-6 becomes 0-0, and 3-3 stays 3-3. You see the result before confirming. The bone stays private and you don't have to play it this turn. Each copy gives one use per hand.

Once per hand, drag any number of pips across a bone's divider. Values stay within 0–6. The shuffled bone becomes public and must be played this turn. Once per hand, move any number of pips across a bone's divider , keeping the total the same and every half between 0 and 6. A 1-5 could become 0-6, 2-4 or 3-3. As with Pip Shift , you can only confirm a result that can be played now, the bone becomes public, and you must play it this turn. More copies do not add uses; it stays once per hand.

With one bone left, draw one extra face-down candidate per stack, reveal them, and choose what to keep. When you go to the boneyard holding exactly one bone , you pick one extra face-down bone for each copy . All of them are turned over and you choose which to keep. It stacks with Sovereign Draw and Light Fingers : their extra picks add together.

On a scoring play, repeat your previous perk bonus. On a scoring play, Echo Chamber adds your most recent perk bonus again , once for each copy. "Most recent" means the last bonus line added on your previous play that had one, after Midas Touch doubling. It can come from an earlier hand in the same match. When Echo Chamber fires, the echo itself becomes your most recent bonus. With two or more copies the echo grows from play to play. Nothing is repeated until you have earned at least one perk bonus.

Every third consecutive play made without drawing adds 15 points if it is a scoring play. Every third play in a row without drawing (your 3rd, 6th, 9th and so on) gains +15 points for each copy if it scores. The count includes plays that didn't score. Drawing, a Table Pass , passing on an empty boneyard and a new hand all reset it.

Each non-scoring play banks a charge. Your next scoring play with an open-end total of 5 gains 5 points per charge. Every one of your plays that does not score banks one charge for each copy. Your next play whose open ends add up to exactly 5 gains +5 points per banked charge , and the bank empties. Plays that score 10, 15 or more neither add to nor spend the bank. Any play with a total of exactly 5 empties the bank, even if Five Jinx wipes the points. The bank resets at the start of every hand. Worked example With one copy you make three plays that don't score, then hit a total of 5: 5 + 15 =

Your opponent's playable bones glow while remaining face-down. Rival's bones that could be played on the board right now glow , while staying face-down. You learn how many of Rival's bones fit the table, though not which numbers they show. The glow updates as the board changes. Extra copies change nothing.

Your remaining pips can never score for your opponent. When you lose a hand, your remaining bones award the winner nothing . It works on both blocked hands and when the winner goes domino. It overrides every other hand award effect, including Heavy Hand and Exposed Hand .

Once per round, explicitly arm one otherwise-illegal play on any open end; spend the charge only when played. Arm Master Key, then play any bone on any open end , even if the numbers don't match. The bone keeps its printed numbers. A compact key icon marks affected landing previews. The status column shows the armed perk and remaining uses; hover or focus a landing for the outcome. The charge is only spent by a play that would otherwise be illegal. An ordinary play cancels the arming and keeps the charge. A double still cannot be played against a double. Each copy gives one use per hand.

Reveal your opponent's rack and choose both bones to swap. After use, wait through the next hand before using it again. See Rival's whole rack , then choose one of your bones and one of Rival's bones to swap. Once per hand however many copies you hold. After you use it, it rests for the next hand and is ready again the hand after that. Using it does not end your turn. Unlike Table Thief , the traded bones are not revealed to the table.

Once per round, arm it before you play. If that play scores, immediately play again. Arm Time Loop before you play. If that play scores, you immediately take another turn . The charge is only spent when the armed play scores. If it doesn't, the arming ends and the charge is kept for later. Each copy gives one use per hand. If the armed play was your last bone, the hand simply ends. With Stumble , the extra turn begins with Stumble's required draw.

When you trail by at least 30 points, your scoring plays are doubled. While you are 30 or more points behind Rival (before the play), your scoring plays are doubled for each copy . It doubles the whole play: open ends, bonuses and any Golden Double doubling. Maluses are applied after it.

Once per hand per stack, play on any double's short side after one long side is filled. This opens its short sides for Four Winds holders. Normally a double only opens its short sides once both long sides are covered. Four Winds lets you play on a double's short side as soon as one long side is covered. Each copy gives one early opening per hand. It works on any double on the table, whoever played it. Once a double has been opened this way, its short sides stay open for every player who holds Four Winds. The new branch counts toward the open ends like any other branch.

On a scoring play, all point bonuses from perks are doubled. On a scoring play, all point bonuses from perks are doubled for each copy: two copies make them four times as large. The open-end total itself is not doubled, only the perk bonuses. Skill bonuses such as Coffin Corner and the points Pip Shield gives back are not doubled either. Golden Double and The Equalizer come after Midas Touch, so they double its result again. Worked example Ends total 20 with Double Trouble (+5) and Hot Streak (+5): 20 + 10 = 30. Midas Touch adds another 10, so the play scores 40 . If it was a double and you al

Every boneyard visit draws one extra face-down candidate per stack; reveal them and choose what to keep. On every boneyard visit you pick one extra face-down bone for each copy . All of them are turned over and you choose which to keep. The rest stay in the boneyard. It stacks with Dead Man's Draw and Light Fingers .

Play locations reveal whether they expand or restrict your opponent's legal options. While you hold a bone, each place you could play it shows whether that play would give Rival more, fewer or the same number of playable bones , judged against Rival's real rack. With two or more copies it shows the exact difference, such as "Rival plays −2".

When your opponent holds one bone, the safest legal play location is marked. When Rival is down to one bone , the safest legal place for the bone you hold is marked. "Blocks rival" means Rival's last bone can't be played after your play. "Safest play" means the play that leaves Rival the smallest scoring reply. Extra copies change nothing.

Your opponent gains 5 extra points from your remaining hand. Malus. When you lose a hand, the winner gets 5 extra points for each copy on top of your remaining pips. It applies after Bone Fortress and Soft Landing and before Exposed Hand . Untouchable Hand cancels it, and Malus Ward can block it.

Every forced draw takes one additional bone. Malus. Every boneyard draw makes you keep one extra bone for each copy . If the boneyard runs short, you take what is left. Malus Ward can block it on one draw.

A scoring double loses 5 points. Malus. A scoring play made with a double loses 5 points for each copy , after every bonus and multiplier. It can't take the play below zero. Pip Shield can give the points back, and Malus Ward can block it.

Every visit to the boneyard costs you 2 points. Malus. Every time you draw from the boneyard you lose 2 points for each copy from your match score. Your score never drops below zero. Passing because the boneyard is empty is not a draw and costs nothing. Pip Shield does not cover it. Malus Ward can block it.

Your highest-pip bone is anchored whenever another play exists. Malus. Your highest-pip bone can't be played while you have any other legal play . You can play it once it is your only option. The rack recalculates every turn, so the anchored bone changes as you play. Malus Ward does not affect it.

An open-end total of exactly 5 scores nothing. Malus. A play whose open ends add up to exactly 5 scores nothing , bonuses included. Totals of 10, 15 and more are unaffected. Extra copies change nothing. Pip Shield gives back up to 5 points per copy, and Malus Ward can block it.

Each perk bonus loses 1 point. Malus. Every bonus on a scoring play costs 1 point for each copy of Perk Tax . Each bonus line on the play counts once, including multiplier lines such as Midas Touch , Golden Double and The Equalizer . Perk Tax can never take a play below its open-end total, and it never adds points. A play with no bonuses is not taxed. Pip Shield can give the points back, and Malus Ward can block it. Worked example Ends total 10 with Double Trouble and Even Flow : 10 + 10 = 20. Two bonus lines and one copy of Perk Tax: the play scores 18 .

The award from your remaining hand increases by 25 percent. Malus. When you lose a hand, the award from your remaining bones goes up 25% for each copy (copies compound: two copies are ×1.5625), rounded up. It applies last, after Bone Fortress , Soft Landing and Heavy Hand . The award is then rounded up to a multiple of five. Untouchable Hand cancels it, and Malus Ward can block it.

After scoring, automatically draw on your next turn whenever possible. Malus. After any play that scores for you , your next turn starts with an automatic boneyard draw . The game explains that Stumble caused it and plays the Malus sound. After that draw you may play as normal. Other draw effects still apply. If they reveal several candidates, you choose which bones to keep. Once the boneyard is empty the requirement lifts and you play normally. You can't use Catch and Release on this draw. Malus Ward can block it. Extra copies change nothing.

Perks are the cards you draft during a match. Each one bends the rules of the table for the rest of that match: extra points, peeks at hidden bones, swaps, wild plays and more. Maluses are the red cards that bend the rules against you. Every perk below links to a page with its exact behaviour, how copies stack and a worked example where the maths matters. Common Uncommon Rare Epic Legendary Malus Some quick rules that apply to every perk: Copies stack. Drafting the same perk twice usually doubles its effect or its uses. Each perk page says exactly how its copies combine. A scoring play is any

Skip one required boneyard draw and yield the turn. Usable only when you have no legal play. Use it on your turn when you have no legal play and the boneyard still has bones. Instead of drawing, you skip the draw and your turn passes to Rival. It is only offered when a draw would otherwise be required. It counts as a trip to the boneyard for perks: your play streaks reset and Lucky Pocket is ready for your next play. Handy when the boneyard is full of bones you don't want, or when Leaky Pocket or Greedy Draw would make a draw expensive.

Earn 25% more XP throughout your next match. Activate it from the Inventory between matches. Your next match earns 25% more XP from every source. Activating another boost adds its matches to the queue instead of raising the bonus, so two Quick Study 1s cover two matches. A queued boost is used by the next match you start in a mode that allows supplies. You can't activate a boost while a match is in progress or saved.
Earn 25% more XP throughout your next three matches. Same as Quick Study 1, but it covers your next three matches with +25% XP.
Earn 25% more XP throughout your next five matches. Same as Quick Study 1, but it covers your next five matches with +25% XP.

Earn 50% more Bone Bucks throughout your next match. Activate it from the Inventory between matches. Your next match earns 50% more Bone Bucks . Like Quick Study, extra activations add matches to the queue rather than raising the bonus.
Earn 50% more Bone Bucks throughout your next three matches. Same as Golden Ledger I, but it covers your next three matches .
Earn 50% more Bone Bucks throughout your next five matches. Same as Golden Ledger I, but it covers your next five matches .

Change every blank half on one bone to a value from one to six. On 0-0, both halves change. The Epic pips determine placement and scoring. On your turn, choose one of your bones with a blank and pick a number from 1 to 6: every blank half on that bone becomes that number . On the double blank both halves change, so 0-0 can become 6-6. The bone keeps its new numbers for placement and scoring, and the game picks it up ready to play. It needs a blank bone in your hand.

For one trip to the boneyard, one fixed face-down bone is revealed. Use it in the hand setup screen before a hand. On your next trip to the boneyard , one random face-down bone is shown face-up before you choose. If you don't visit the boneyard that hand, the light waits for your next visit in the same match. The Boneyard Lantern perk does the same on every visit.

After an unplayable draw, inspect a second fixed bone and choose which one to keep. When you draw a single bone that cannot be played and the boneyard still has another bone, the game offers to spend a Rail Pass. You then pick a second face-down bone, both are turned over, and you keep the one you want . It is only offered on a plain one-bone draw. If you decline, the draw finishes normally.

Reduce one open end by one for the next scoring calculation. The board itself does not change. On your turn, choose an open end. On your next play , that end counts one pip less when the table adds up the open ends. The bone on the table doesn't change. Use it to turn a total such as 16 into a scoring 15. The erased end has to still be open after your play. If you play on that end it is covered, nothing is erased, and the Pip Eraser is still spent. Forecasts and scoring highlights include the armed reduction in solo and online play. The flying count at that end shows its reduced contribution.

If you win this hand and pass the hammer, your compensation draft has improved rarity odds. Use it in the hand setup screen. If you win that hand and pass the hammer to Rival, your compensation draft has better rarity odds : commons become much less likely and every higher rarity more likely. It is spent when you use it. If you lose the hand, or win and keep the hammer, it is wasted. See Matches, hands and drafts for the hammer and the compensation draft.

Wager one eligible supply before a hand. Win to receive two copies; lose and it is gone. Use it in the hand setup screen and stake one of your supplies : a supply you own at least one of, that isn't at its holding limit, and isn't another Dealer's Dare. Win the hand: you get two copies of the staked supply, up to its holding limit. That's one more than you staked. Lose the hand: the staked copy is gone. Dealer's Dare itself is used up either way.

Reveal the current total of every exposed end during play. Shows the current total of all open ends on the table at all times, so you can see at a glance how far you are from the next multiple of five.
Highlight every bone in your hand that can be played. Every bone in your rack that can be played right now is highlighted, so you never have to hunt for a legal play.
Make valid gray drop boxes glow when you select a bone. When you pick up a bone, every valid drop box for it glows. Drop boxes that need the bone rotated are marked "Rotate to play".

Scoring play locations flare pink before you commit. When you pick up a bone, the places where it would score flare pink before you commit, and the tooltip shows the base score. An armed Pip Eraser is included when its targeted end will remain open after the play, in both solo and online matches.

Show projected open-end totals before you commit a play. Hovering a place to play shows the open-end total the table would have after that play, even when it would not score. Compact number badges sit beside the landing previews, with one Projected totals caption in the status column. The bones stay visible; a crowded table keeps the forecast available in the landing tooltip. Compact projected-total numbers sit beside the landing previews, with one shared caption and armed status. Totals include an armed Pip Eraser reduction while its target stays open. Covering that end removes the deduction

Count how many unplayed bones outside your rack contain each pip, including public bones Rival still holds. Shows, for each number from 0 to 6, how many bones you haven't seen played yet contain that number : bones in Rival's rack and in the boneyard. Bones Rival has revealed are included. It is a counting aid: it never shows where a bone is.

Hover plays for follow-up counts. Rank 1 marks the best location. Rank 2 labels its count. Rank 3 also marks your best hand bone blue; scoring breaks ties. Hovering a place to play shows how many follow-up plays your rack would have afterwards. Rank 1 marks the location that leaves you the most follow-ups. Rank 2 also labels that count on the board. Rank 3 also marks your best bone to play in blue. When two options are tied, the one that scores wins.

A scoring play that fills the fourth side of a spinner gains 10 points per rank. A scoring play that fills the fourth and last side of a spinner gains +10 points per rank . The bonus is added after maluses, and only if the play still scores. It is a skill bonus, so Midas Touch doesn't double it.

Increase the relative odds of uncommon or better perks by 12% per rank. Raises the relative odds of Uncommon, Rare, Epic and Legendary cards in your perk drafts by 12% per rank. Commons become correspondingly less frequent. Legendary perks still only appear once you have unlocked them.
Further increase rare and epic perk odds by 15% per rank. Raises the relative odds of Rare, Epic and Legendary cards by a further 15% per rank, on top of Loaded Luck .
Further increase unlocked legendary perk odds by 25% per rank. Raises the relative odds of Legendary cards by a further 25% per rank. It only affects legendary perks you have already unlocked.

House of Pips Wiki House of Pips is a domino roguelike. You play Five-Up style dominoes against Rival, scoring whenever the open ends of the table add up to a multiple of five, and between hands you draft perks that bend the rules in your favour, alongside the maluses that bend them against you. This wiki explains every rule, perk, supply, skill and mode in House of Pips, with the same names, rarities and numbers you see on screen. The main menu of a brand-new career. Rival and table styles Rival is your opponent across the table in solo matches. He drafts perks and maluses from the same cards you do, and his perks have the same effects as yours. When Rival uses a perk, the table pauses on a notice so you can see what happened; the ledger records it too. Skill levels # Rival sits down at one of three skill levels. In Custom mode you choose the level. Skill level In the game Casual Easygoing company. Rival plays loose and leaves openings. Strategic A sharper opponent. Domino rules House of Pips plays the scoring game Nana calls Five-Up : a game of matching dominoes where you score whenever the open ends of the table add up to a multiple of five. This page covers the plain rules. Perks, skills and supplies change many of them; their pages say exactly how. A hand in progress: your rack at the bottom, Rival's face-down rack at the top, scores and perks along the sides. The bones # The game uses one double-six set : 28 bones, every pairing of the numbers 0 to 6 exactly once. Each half shows 0 to 6 pips . A bone whose halves match (such as 4-4) is a double ; the

Saving, Continue and Steam Cloud Your career saves itself # Your career (level, skills, Bone Bucks, unlocks, supplies, cosmetics and records) is saved on your computer as you play. There is no manual save. Matches save automatically # An unfinished match is saved whenever the table settles after a change, and closing the window keeps it. Next time, CONTINUE on the main menu takes you back exactly where you left the table. Scoring in depth Most of the time a play scores its open-end total plus a few perk bonuses. When several perks and maluses meet on one play, the order they apply in decides the result. This page lists that order for scoring plays and for the hand award. Which plays score # A play scores when, after your bone is placed, the open ends add up to a positive multiple of five . Perk bonuses can only add to a play that already scores; no perk turns a total of 12 into a scoring play. (The Pip Eraser supply is the exception: it lowers the total before this check, so it can turn 16 into a scoring 15.) R
